May does not come—

May does not come.

**Interpretation:**

The repetition of “May does not come” functions as a rhythmic, almost obsessive lament, emphasizing the unbroken absence of the expected month. The middle line, “my heart opened,” does not suggest joyful expansion but rather a raw, involuntary exposure—the heart is forced open by the strain of waiting. The speaker’s emotional world is laid bare precisely because the natural world refuses to deliver its promised renewal. The seasonal cycle, typically a source of comfort or rhythm, becomes a source of torment: the arrival of May is anticipated as a relief or a turning point, yet it never materializes. This creates a sense of temporal dislocation, where time seems stuck in a perpetual pre-spring limbo. The haiku’s brevity mirrors the constriction of the soul, compressing an entire season of hope and despair into seventeen syllables.

**Literary criticism:**  
From this perspective, the poem’s formal elements reinforce its theme of thwarted expectation. The anaphoric structure—the identical phrase bookending the middle line—creates a circular, trapped movement, as if the speaker cannot escape the thought of May’s failure. The grammatical ambiguity of “来ぬ” (which could also be read as the perfective “has come”) is not resolved; instead, the repetition forces both readings to coexist, generating a discordant tension between what is hoped for and what actually occurs. The poem thus critiques the naive expectation that nature’s cycles bring comfort, revealing instead how those cycles can become a source of existential dread when they fail to align with human need. The lack of any specific natural imagery (no blossoms, no rain, no moon) heightens the abstract, psychological quality of the desperation—it is not a particular feature of May that is missed, but the very idea of May’s arrival as an anchor for hope. In this reading, the haiku becomes a stark meditation on the fragility of human reliance on seasonal order.

The seasonal word “立春” traditionally signals rebirth, yet it is subordinated to the rain, which becomes a symbol of entropy and despair. The poem does not argue for hope but presents hope as an illusion that highlights the inescapable truth of darkness. The imagery remains visually concrete yet emotionally abstract, forcing the reader to sit with the discomfort of a promise that can never be fulfilled.
